p: Born on 4 September 1881, he married Lalla Jeneïna Beya, the daughter of a Tripolitanian merchant of Tunis, in 1902. On 25 June 1942 Moncef Bey named him Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent. A month later he warned Moncef that the court counsellor General M'hammed Belkhodja was urging the French Resident General Jean-Pierre Esteva to depose him.

In May 1943 General Alphonse Juin came to Tunis with orders to remove Moncef Bey for alleged attempts to collaborate with the Axis forces. Juin found no grounds for condemning him. Lamine at first refused to promise that he would accept the throne and agreed largely because of the benefits to his family. Juin installed him at the Bardo palace on 15 May 1943. Moncef abdicated only on 6 July.

For most Tunisians he remained a usurper, the Bey of the French. The other Husainid princes boycotted him. The death of Moncef Bey in exile on 1 September 1948 removed the possibility of a restoration, and his subjects began to regard him as their legitimate ruler.

He then worked clandestinely with Habib Bourguiba and Salah Ben Youssef for self-government. In 1952 the Resident General Jean de Hauteclocque imprisoned Bourguiba and had the Bey's ministers arrested; the Bey refused to sign decrees, bringing government to a standstill, and gave way after the trade union leader Farhat Hached was assassinated in December 1952. In 1954 he accepted a reform package negotiated by Muhammad Salah Mzali while Bourguiba was still confined. After the French Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France announced internal autonomy on 31 July 1954, France dealt with the Neo Destour alone.

As king he signed without protest the decree of 31 May 1956 that abolished the privileges of the ruling family. On 15 July 1957 the Tunisian army replaced the Royal Guard around the palace, and on 25 July the Constituent Assembly voted by a show of hands to abolish the monarchy.

He was taken with members of his family to an abandoned palace in Manouba without water or electricity; two of his sons and his son-in-law were imprisoned. In October 1958 he and his wife were moved to a small villa in La Soukra, still under house arrest. She died two days after three days of interrogation about the family jewels, and his confinement was then lifted. He died in Tunis on 30 September 1962 and was buried beside her in the cemetery of Sidi Abdelaziz in La Marsa, not in the dynasty's mausoleum of Tourbet el Bey.

notes: The article's family list gives three princes and nine princesses, but its narrative of 25 July 1957 says 'three sons, seven daughters'; I left the number of children out.
The article dates Bourguiba's Eid al-Fitr visit '19 July' in a paragraph about 1956-1957 without a clear year; left out.
The year of his wife's death is given only as 'two years later' after a 1958 trial date; I gave no year.
Sons imprisoned: Chedly and Ben Salem (son-in-law) at Kairouan, Salah Eddine in Tunis: hence 'two of his sons and his son-in-law'.
